statement: Acute psychosocial stress lowers alpha. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis found alpha power, mainly frontal, decreasing consistently (Hedges’ g = 0.6, p = 0.001; 10 of 12 articles reported significant decreases), beta tending to rise without a significant pooled effect (g = −0.31 in the review’s sign convention, p = 0.29; 6 of 8 articles reported increases) and frontal alpha asymmetry not changing consistently (g = 0.01); after a 10 min Stroop stressor and after 30 h of sleep deprivation in 30 adults, high-alpha (11 to 12 Hz) relative power fell and high-beta (23 to 36 Hz) rose, strongest anteriorly, with no significant asymmetry change.
sources: Vanhollebeke G, De Smet S, De Raedt R, Baeken C, van Mierlo P, Vanderhasselt M-A (2022). The neural correlates of psychosocial stress: A systematic review and meta-analysis of spectral analysis EEG studies. Neurobiology of Stress 18:100452. doi:10.1016/j.ynstr.2022.100452

note_for_auditor: Vanhollebeke 2022 (open, Neurobiology of Stress): g = 0.6, p = 0.001, 10 of 12, beta g = −0.31 p = 0.29, 6 of 8, FAA g = 0.01. Alonso 2015 (author postprint on upcommons.upc.edu): the Stroop and sleep-deprivation design, 30 adults, high alpha 11–12 Hz down, high beta 23–36 Hz up, anterior, asymmetry not significant.

statement: Meditation has no universal EEG signature. In 34 older novices after a 6-week course, 15 min of mindfulness meditation against 15 min of listening to a podcast, both with eyes closed, raised theta and beta power over most regions (occipital theta 291 against 171 µV²/Hz) and alpha only at occipital and right temporal sites (329 against 300), with frontal theta and alpha unchanged; experienced practitioners of nondirective meditation showed higher theta (largest frontal and temporal-central) and alpha (largest posterior) than in eyes-closed rest; but 16 long-term Vipassana meditators showed no theta or alpha change against instructed mind wandering, and 10 Theravada practitioners had lower alpha during meditation than at rest. Consumer “calm” scores most likely reward alpha and theta, and a 2025 meta-analysis of 16 randomized trials (763 participants) found no evidence that users modulate those targets.
sources: Ahani A, Wahbeh H, Nezamfar H, Miller M, Erdogmus D, Oken B (2014). Quantitative change of EEG and respiration signals during mindfulness meditation. Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation 11:87. doi:10.1186/1743-0003-11-87

statement: Deliberate relaxation has no single EEG signature. A systematic review of slow-breathing studies reports higher alpha and lower theta power than during spontaneous breathing (clearest in 22 people breathing 3 to 4 times a minute with eyes closed); a randomized comparison of a recorded relaxation technique with music after 6 weeks found larger theta increases with the technique and called theta, not alpha, the more reliable marker; and the relaxation response in 20 novices reduced frontal beta only, with no alpha or theta change in any region.
sources: Zaccaro A, Piarulli A, Laurino M, Garbella E, Menicucci D, Neri B, Gemignani A (2018). How Breath-Control Can Change Your Life: A Systematic Review on Psycho-Physiological Correlates of Slow Breathing. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 12:353. doi:10.3389/fnhum.2018.00353

statement: Emotional valence is read from frontal alpha asymmetry, the log alpha power on the right (F4) minus the left (F3), and its state effects are small. In 33 students watching four emotional film clips, baseline-normalized alpha at F3 and F4 differed between emotions by about 0.1 against between-person standard deviations of about 0.3, and alpha was higher at F4 than at F3 for positive and negative clips alike; in the 32-participant DEAP dataset no alpha electrode correlated with valence ratings at p < 0.01 (mean correlations seldom above ±0.1) and single-trial valence classification from EEG reached 57.6% against 50%; in the original film study, disgust showed right-sided frontal and anterior temporal activation relative to happiness only in epochs selected by facial expression, with no reliable difference for pooled positive against negative films. Resting asymmetry is about 60% stable trait and 40% occasion-specific state (59 people, four sessions), and its split-half reliability reaches 0.90 with about 80 s of clean data (204 people).
